tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Records of Arrest, Dismissal of Charges or Disposition (Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1401)
tracks.publicName: Clear an arrest or dismissed charge

controllingAuthority.summary: On a verified petition to the court in which the proceeding occurred or would have occurred, the court may expunge records of an arrest, a charge that was dismissed, or a disposition where the person was not convicted, provided at least 180 days have passed, no formal charges are pending, and no disposition under § 7-13-301, § 35-7-1037 or former § 7-13-203 was entered to any charge arising from the incident, including to a different or lesser charge. Expungement classifies the record at the Division of Criminal Investigation so it is not disseminated except to criminal justice agencies for criminal justice purposes; the court file is sealed and a certified order is transmitted to DCI.

exclusions: Any disposition under Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-301, § 35-7-1037 or former § 7-13-203 entered to any charge resulting from the incident, including a disposition to a different or lesser charge.
Formal charges pending against the person at the time the petition is filed.

Records that are not maintained in the state central repository at the Division of Criminal Investigation, including investigatory files of any local, state or federal criminal justice agency used solely for criminal justice purposes.
Federal, tribal and out-of-state records, which Wyoming relief does not reach.

destination.detail: File the verified petition and the proposed Order for Expungement with the clerk of that court. Serve the prosecuting attorney. No filing fee applies under § 7-13-1401. components.notes: Petition for Expungement (W.S. 7-13-1401). Wyoming publishes no statewide expungement form, so this is drafted. Caption the underlying criminal case where one exists, with the participant identified as the defendant. Where no charges were filed and there is no case number, the petition opens a new matter and the clerk assigns the number. Cite only § 7-13-1401; do not blend the three Wyoming expungement statutes in one petition.

Order for Expungement, which the Wyoming Judicial Branch expects the petitioner to have ready for the judge's signature. The order directs that the court file be placed under seal, available for inspection only by order of the court, and that a certified copy be transmitted to the Division of Criminal Investigation. The order is proposed and is generated unexecuted: its findings, its date, the judge's signature block and every clerk or court execution field are left blank, and nothing in it asserts that the court has acted. It is prepared so it is available to the court; whether it goes in with the initial filing or is brought later is that court's filing practice.
Verification block. Section 7-13-1401 requires the petition to be verified by the petitioner; this is not optional.
Certificate of service on the prosecuting attorney. The 20-day objection window runs from service, so the service date governs when an order may issue.

Filing, service and timing sheet: call the clerk about local templates and formatting before finalizing; file; serve the prosecuting attorney; no order may issue before 20 days after service; if the prosecutor objects the court sets a hearing; if no objection the court may summarily enter the order on finding eligibility. No civil summons and no praecipe are required on this route under the statewide statutes and published guidance, and neither is generated. The clerk call covers local filing mechanics only — cover sheet, copy count, electronic or paper filing, chambers copy, and whether the proposed order goes in with the initial filing or is brought later — because Wyoming publishes no statewide form for either document and there is no local template outside Casper Municipal Court that this route uses.

rules.filing: File the verified Petition for Expungement and the proposed Order for Expungement with the clerk of the court in which the proceeding occurred or would have occurred. Wyoming publishes no statewide petition form and no statewide proposed-order template, so both documents are drafted and are complete as drafted. Call that clerk about that court's own filing mechanics — cover sheet, copy count, electronic or paper filing, whether a chambers copy is wanted, and whether the proposed order is submitted with the initial filing or brought later — not about whether the document itself is right.
rules.notice: The prosecuting attorney reviews the petition. No order may be granted before the expiration of 20 days after service on the prosecuting attorney. If the prosecutor objects the court sets a hearing; if no objection is filed the court may summarily enter the order on finding the petitioner eligible.
rules.service: Serve the verified petition on the prosecuting attorney and file proof of service. The Division of Criminal Investigation is not a service recipient on this track.
rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs and verifies the petition. Verification by the petitioner is required by statute.
rules.notarization: Verification is required by statute; confirm with the clerk of the filing court whether that court requires the verification to be sworn before a notary.

A completed felony deferral. Section 7-13-1401 is barred by the deferral and § 7-13-1502 by its terms requires a conviction, so there may be no Wyoming route at all. Stop and refer to a lawyer.
The prosecuting attorney files an objection, or the court sets a contested hearing.
Criminal charges are pending against the participant.
Facts indicating human trafficking or coercion, which route to the § 6-2-708 vacatur outside this track.
Any offense subject to sex offender registration.
Immigration consequences.
Federal, tribal or out-of-state records.
Records of a juvenile matter, which are handled under Wyo. Stat. § 14-6-241 and § 14-6-440 outside this track.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The cleanest track in Wyoming: no filing fee, no substantial-danger finding, no lifetime cap, a 180-day wait, and a summary-entry path where the prosecuting attorney does not object. The review approved it for implementation without limitation, and identifies it as the volume product for the state. Wyoming publishes no statewide petition form, so the track is a custom pleading; that is the settled classification for the jurisdiction rather than a gap.

limitations.statement: Wyoming publishes no statewide expungement form. County clerks, municipal courts and circuit courts may have local templates or formatting requirements. Call the clerk of the court where the petition will be filed before finalizing, and use a local template where one exists. Never invent a statewide form number.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Records of Conviction of Certain Misdemeanors (Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1501)

controllingAuthority.summary: A person who has pled guilty or nolo contendere to, or been convicted of, a misdemeanor may petition the convicting court to expunge the records of conviction. The waiting period is at least five years for non-status offenses and at least one year for status offenses as defined by § 7-1-107(b)(iii), measured from expiration of the terms of sentence including probation and any court-ordered program. The offense must not have involved the use or attempted use of a firearm; a health care provider convicted of a § 6-2-313 offense against a patient in their care is ineligible. The court must find the petitioner is not a substantial danger to himself, any identifiable victim or society. One expungement under this section is permitted in a lifetime. Per the Wyoming Judicial Branch, the section includes cases of deferred adjudication and cases where the charge was later dismissed.

exclusions: Misdemeanors involving the use or attempted use of a firearm.
A health care provider who pled guilty or nolo contendere to, or was convicted of, an offense punishable under Wyo. Stat. § 6-2-313 committed against a patient under that provider's care.
Any person who has previously received an expungement of records of conviction under § 7-13-1501; the statute permits one in a lifetime.
Felony convictions, which are handled under § 7-13-1502.
Federal, tribal and out-of-state records, which Wyoming relief does not reach.

A juvenile Child in Need of Supervision adjudication under Wyo. Stat. § 14-6-402(a)(iv) — habitual truancy as defined in § 21-4-101(a)(ii), running away from home, habitually disobeying the reasonable and lawful demands of a parent, guardian, custodian or other proper authority, or being ungovernable and beyond control. Section 7-13-1501(a) reaches only a person who has pled guilty or nolo contendere to, or been convicted of, a misdemeanor, and a CHINS adjudication is none of those three things. It is outside the section whichever waiting period the word "status" might suggest.

waitingPeriods.condition: Non-status misdemeanor offense. This is the default branch and it takes every offense the section reaches other than one the legislature has itself labelled a status offense. Wyo. Stat. § 7-1-107(b)(iii) expressly excludes a violation of § 12-6-101(b) or (c), or any similar municipal ordinance, from the definition, so an under-twenty-one alcohol conviction under § 12-6-101(c) — purchase, attempted purchase, solicitation, possession, consumption, a measurable alcohol concentration, unaccompanied presence in a designated off-premise sales area, or dispensing or selling — takes this five-year branch and not the one-year branch. Convictions under § 6-4-305(c) or (d) are ordinary misdemeanors by § 6-4-305(f) and take this branch too. The branch is decided from the Revised Statutes section of conviction shown on the judgment and sentence, never from the participant's age at the time, never from the case having been in juvenile court, and never from the offense merely being minor.
waitingPeriods.duration: At least 5 years since the expiration of the terms of the sentence imposed by the court, including any period of probation or completion of any program ordered by the court

waitingPeriods.condition: Status offense as defined by Wyo. Stat. § 7-1-107(b)(iii): an offense which, if committed by an adult, would not constitute an act punishable as a criminal offense by the laws of this state or a violation of a municipal ordinance, but which does not include a violation of W.S. 12-6-101(b) or (c) or any similar municipal ordinance. The one offense the Wyoming legislature has expressly labelled a status offense under that definition is W.S. 6-4-305(b) — a minor who knowingly disseminates a nude image of himself, or possesses a nude image of another minor at least eleven years of age, subject to the inadvertent-possession exception — because § 6-4-305(e) says so in terms and uses this same cross-reference. A conviction recorded under § 6-4-305(b) takes this one-year branch. This branch is the exception and must be justified from the charging section.
waitingPeriods.duration: At least 1 year since the expiration of the terms of the sentence imposed by the court, including any period of probation or completion of any program ordered by the court

destination.name: The Wyoming convicting court
destination.detail: File the verified petition and the proposed Order for Expungement with the clerk of the convicting court and pay the $100 filing fee per petition. Serve the prosecuting attorney and the Division of Criminal Investigation. The prosecutor notifies identifiable victims. On grant the court seals the file and transmits a certified copy of the order to DCI.

components.notes: Petition for Expungement of Records of Conviction (W.S. 7-13-1501). Wyoming publishes no statewide form. Caption the underlying criminal case with the participant identified as the defendant. Cite only § 7-13-1501; the three Wyoming routes have different elements and a petition that blends them invites denial.

Order for Expungement for the judge's signature, directing that the court file be sealed and available for inspection only by order of the court, and that a certified copy be transmitted to the Division of Criminal Investigation. The order is proposed and is generated unexecuted: its findings, its date, the judge's signature block and every clerk or court execution field are left blank, and nothing in it asserts that the court has acted. It is prepared so it is available to the court; whether it goes in with the initial filing or is brought later is that court's filing practice.
Verification block. Section 7-13-1501 requires the petition to be verified by the petitioner.
Certificate of service on the prosecuting attorney and on the Division of Criminal Investigation. The 30-day objection window runs from service on the prosecuting attorney.

Filing, fee, service and timing sheet, including the $100 fee, the two service recipients, the 30-day objection window for the prosecutor or a victim, the possibility of a hearing where the court requests a DCI report and the petitioner objects to it, and the once-per-lifetime disclosure. No civil summons and no praecipe are required on this route under the statewide statutes and published guidance, and neither is generated. Notice to identifiable victims is given by the prosecuting attorney. It is outside-party work: this packet neither generates it nor completes it, and nothing in the packet asserts that it has happened. The clerk call covers local filing mechanics only — cover sheet, copy count, electronic or paper filing, chambers copy, and whether the proposed order goes in with the initial filing or is brought later — because Wyoming publishes no statewide form for either document and there is no local template outside Casper Municipal Court that this route uses.

Have you ever received an expungement of a misdemeanor conviction in Wyoming under this statute before?
Was there an identifiable victim in this case?
Do you know whether this conviction appears on your Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation criminal history?

rules.filing: File the verified Petition for Expungement of Records of Conviction and the proposed Order for Expungement with the clerk of the convicting court. Wyoming publishes no statewide petition form and no statewide proposed-order template, so both documents are drafted and are complete as drafted. Call that clerk about that court's own filing mechanics — cover sheet, copy count, electronic or paper filing, whether a chambers copy is wanted, and whether the proposed order is submitted with the initial filing or brought later — not about whether the document itself is right.
rules.notice: The prosecuting attorney and any identifiable victim have 30 days to object; the prosecutor, not the petitioner, notifies identifiable victims. A hearing is also set where the court requests a report from the Division of Criminal Investigation and the petitioner objects to it. The court must find both that the petitioner is eligible and that the petitioner does not represent a substantial danger to himself, any identifiable victim or society before issuing the order.

rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs and verifies the petition. Verification by the petitioner is required by statute.
rules.notarization: Verification is required by statute; confirm with the clerk of the convicting court whether that court requires the verification to be sworn before a notary.

statusOffenseDetermination.definitionVerbatim: "Status offense" means an offense which, if committed by an adult, would not constitute an act punishable as a criminal offense by the laws of this state or a violation of a municipal ordinance, but does not include a violation of W.S. 12-6-101(b) or (c) or any similar municipal ordinance.
statusOffenseDetermination.definitionLocation: Wyo. Stat. § 7-1-107(b)(iii). Subsection (b) opens "As used in W.S. 7-1-107 and 7-1-108", which are juvenile-detention sections, but § 7-13-1501(a)(i) does not rely on the definition applying of its own force: it borrows it by section, subsection and paragraph. The borrowing carries the definition and not the juvenile context, and § 7-13-1501 applies to persons rather than to minors.
statusOffenseDetermination.doNotReachForTheTitle14Definitions: W.S. 14-6-201(a)(xxiii) and W.S. 14-6-402(a)(xx) carry nearly identical definitions for their own acts, the latter without the "or any similar municipal ordinance" tail. Neither is the definition § 7-13-1501(a)(i) points at.
statusOffenseDetermination.whatTheTestIs: Counterfactual and stated in the negative: conduct that is an offense only because of who the actor is. The definition then carves one thing back out, and the carve-out is absolute.

oneYearBranch.why: Section 6-4-305(e) provides that a minor convicted of violating subsection (b) "is guilty of a status offense as defined in W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii)". This is the only place in the Wyoming code where the legislature attaches that label to a specific offense, and it uses the same cross-reference § 7-13-1501(a)(i) uses.
oneYearBranch.anchor: One year from the expiration of the terms of sentence imposed by the court, including any period of probation and the completion of any program ordered by the court. The clock does not run from the conviction date, from the offense date or from the sentencing date.

fiveYearBranch.takes: every other offense the section reaches
fiveYearBranch.expresslyIncluded: W.S. 12-6-101(c), the under-twenty-one alcohol offenses, and any similar municipal ordinance. The legislature put them outside the status-offense definition in terms, so they take five years. This is the most consequential single answer on this track, because under-twenty-one alcohol is the charge a participant is most likely to expect to be treated as a youthful status matter. W.S. 6-4-305(c) and (d) are ordinary misdemeanors by § 6-4-305(f) and take five years as well.
fiveYearBranch.anchor: Five years from the expiration of the terms of sentence imposed by the court, including any period of probation and the completion of any program ordered by the court. Same anchor as the one-year branch; only the duration differs.

insideTheDefinitionButNeverReachingThisS.offenses: W.S. 14-3-304, purchase or attempted purchase of nicotine products by a person under twenty-one, and W.S. 14-3-305, possession or use of nicotine products by a person under twenty-one.
insideTheDefinitionButNeverReachingThisS.why: Each section expunges itself. Sections 14-3-304(d) and 14-3-305(e) provide that the court shall not report the conviction to any law enforcement agency and that, on payment of the fine, the conviction shall be expunged by operation of law from all records of the court six months after entry of conviction, after which the conviction is deemed not to have occurred and the individual may reply accordingly upon any inquiry. A participant with such a conviction has nothing left to petition about.
insideTheDefinitionButNeverReachingThisS.andItCostsNothing: Each subsection ends "No expungement under this subsection shall be considered for purposes of any other law providing for expungement", so an automatic nicotine expungement does not consume the once-in-a-lifetime allowance in § 7-13-1501(k). That is worth telling the participant rather than leaving to inference.

outsideTheSectionAltogether.conduct: Habitual truancy under W.S. 21-4-101(a)(ii), running away from home, habitually disobeying the reasonable and lawful demands of a parent, guardian, custodian or other proper authority, and being ungovernable and beyond control.
outsideTheSectionAltogether.why: These are the Child in Need of Supervision grounds in W.S. 14-6-402(a)(iv), dealt with in the juvenile court by adjudication. Section 7-13-1501(a) reaches only a plea of guilty or nolo contendere or a conviction of a misdemeanor, and a CHINS adjudication is none of those.
outsideTheSectionAltogether.careRequired: This is the single most likely mis-screen on this track. A participant who says "I had a truancy case as a kid" is describing a juvenile matter the section does not reach, and the packet must not route them into the one-year branch on the strength of the word.

statusOffenseDetermination.carveOutDefect: The carve-out excludes "a violation of W.S. 12-6-101(b) or (c)", and § 12-6-101(b) was repealed by Laws 2010, ch. 6, § 2. Half the carve-out points at nothing. It changes no outcome, because subsection (c) carries the entire under-twenty-one prohibition, and it is recorded so that a future revisor's correction to § 7-1-107(b)(iii) is read as housekeeping rather than as a change of scope.
statusOffenseDetermination.doAnyOfTheseExceptionsChangePacketAvaila: No. None of them adds or removes a packet, a component, a filing vehicle or a route. The carve-out moves under-twenty-one alcohol from the one-year branch to the five-year branch; the two nicotine sections describe participants who have nothing left to petition about; and CHINS conduct is outside the section and is screened out. The packet Wyoming would build for this track is the same packet either way, which is why the waiting period stops being an undetermined design element.
statusOffenseDetermination.participantInputThatDecidesTheBranch: convictionStatuteSection — the Revised Statutes section of conviction, copied from the judgment and sentence. It is a determinate input the participant can supply from their own record, and it is the only thing that decides the branch.
typedStops: The participant cannot identify the statute section of conviction: fail closed rather than infer the branch.
The conviction is under a municipal ordinance rather than a Wyoming statute: fail closed, because whether the section reaches it at all is unresolved.
The matter was a juvenile CHINS adjudication rather than a misdemeanor plea or conviction: fail closed, because the section does not reach it.

legalEffect.whatSection1501Does: Two things. It expunges the record, which § 7-13-1501(m)(i) defines by adopting § 7-13-1401(j)(i) — the classification of the record held in the state central repository at the Division of Criminal Investigation so that it is not available for dissemination other than to criminal justice agencies of any state or federal criminal justice agencies, for criminal justice purposes only — and under § 7-13-1501(g) the court places its own files under seal, available for inspection only by order of that court.
legalEffect.whatItIsNot: It is not destruction. The record continues to exist and remains available to criminal justice agencies, and the definition expressly does not reach investigatory files of any local, state or federal criminal justice agency used solely for criminal justice purposes.
legalEffect.restoresNothing: Section 7-13-1501 restores no right by its own terms. Its subsection (m) is the definitions subsection, which is what makes the comparison with § 7-13-1502(m) easy to misread: the two sections use the same letter for different things.
legalEffect.andTheOmissionIsDeliberate: As enacted by 2004 ch. 69 the section existed to restore firearm rights and said so in subsection (a), and its catch title was "Restoration of firearm rights-expungement". 2009 ch. 67, whose own title is "amending the purposes for which an expungement under W.S. 7-13-1501 may be used", removed the purpose clause from (a) and the restoration sentence from (k) and replaced the one-year clock with five years. 2018 ch. 80 later turned the section into a general misdemeanor route and added no restoration provision either. The legislature did not forget; it removed it.
legalEffect.doNotCrossRead: Section 7-13-1502(m) may not be read across into § 7-13-1501. The two sections were enacted seven years apart in unrelated acts and are differently drafted throughout, and the one that lacks restoration lost it by amendment. A later editor harmonising the copy across the two conviction tracks would make the misdemeanor packet promise something the statute does not.
legalEffect.answerAsIfEntitlement: Section 7-13-1401(f) lets a person who received an order of expungement "under this section" respond to any inquiry as though the arrest or charge did not occur. It is confined to its own section by its own words, and neither § 7-13-1501 nor § 7-13-1502 has an equivalent. The safe copy on this track is silence.
mayState: That the court will place its files under seal, available for inspection only by order of that court.

That the Division of Criminal Investigation record is reclassified so it is not disseminated other than to criminal justice agencies of any state or federal criminal justice agencies, for criminal justice purposes only.
That the section reaches only the records it defines and does not reach investigatory files held by a criminal justice agency for criminal justice purposes.
That relief is discretionary: the court must find both eligibility and that the petitioner does not represent a substantial danger to himself, any identifiable victim or society.
mustNotState: That firearm rights are restored — the specific promise the section was created to make in 2004 and the specific promise the 2009 act removed.
That the participant may answer an inquiry as though the conviction did not occur.
That the record is destroyed, erased or gone.
legalEffect.federalBoundary: Whether any federal consequence follows from a Wyoming expungement is outside every integrated Wyoming decision and is not asserted in either direction. A participant asking about it is a stop condition rather than a copy problem.

retiredQuestion.priorQuestion: Does an expungement under § 7-13-1501 restore any rights? Section 7-13-1502(m) has an express restoration provision and § 7-13-1501 does not appear to, which changes what may be promised on the misdemeanor track.
retiredQuestion.answer: No right is restored, and the omission is deliberate and traceable to 2009 ch. 67.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Approved for implementation with limitations. Two product rules follow from the review. First, the deferred-adjudication sub-route must be built and surfaced: per the Wyoming Judicial Branch this section includes cases of deferred adjudication and cases later dismissed, so a completed misdemeanor deferral is not a § 7-13-1401 case and is not a dead end — it is a § 7-13-1501 case. That routing is encoded here as an eligibility branch rather than left to a manual-review queue. Second, the once-per-lifetime limit must be disclosed before payment. The status-offense classification is no longer undetermined: the integrated eligibility decision supplies the definition, the one expressly labelled occupant, the expressly carved-out class and the conduct that never reaches the section, so the branch is decided from the Revised Statutes section of conviction and the legal-design blocker that named waiting_period is retired. What now holds this track is a different and prior question the same decision opened — whether a municipal ordinance conviction is a misdemeanor within § 7-13-1501(m)(ii) — which is carried at build level and is not downgraded to make the track buildable.

limitations.statement: The waiting period is decided from the Revised Statutes section of conviction and from nothing else. One year applies where the section of conviction is W.S. 6-4-305(b), which § 6-4-305(e) expressly labels a status offense under § 7-1-107(b)(iii). Five years applies to every other offense the section reaches, including an under-twenty-one alcohol conviction under W.S. 12-6-101(c), which § 7-1-107(b)(iii) expressly excludes from the definition, and including W.S. 6-4-305(c) and (d), which § 6-4-305(f) makes ordinary misdemeanors. Both branches run from the expiration of the terms of sentence imposed by the court, including any period of probation and the completion of any program ordered by the court. Never route the branch on the participant's age at the time, on the case having been in juvenile court, or on the offense sounding minor.

provenance.sourceStatement: The one-year branch is real but narrow. It has exactly one statutorily identified occupant that can produce a live misdemeanour conviction needing expungement: W.S. 6-4-305(b). ... For any Wyoming misdemeanour a participant is likely to bring, the clock is five years from the expiration of the terms of sentence including any period of probation and the completion of any court-ordered programme. ... What drives the branch: the Revised Statutes section the person was convicted under, taken from the court record.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Records of Conviction of Certain Felonies (Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1502)

controllingAuthority.summary: A person convicted of a felony, or of felonies subject to expungement under the section arising out of the same occurrence or related course of events, may petition the convicting court to expunge the records of conviction. At least ten years must have passed since expiration of the terms of sentence including probation; any court-ordered program must be complete and court-ordered restitution paid in full; the petitioner must have no other felony plea, nolo plea or conviction; the offense must not have involved the use or attempted use of a firearm except certain Title 23 offenses; and the offense must not appear on the statutory exclusion list. The court must find eligibility and that the petitioner is not a substantial danger to himself, any identifiable victim or society. One expungement under this section is permitted in a lifetime. Under subsection (m) the expungement restores any rights removed as a result of the conviction.

exclusions: Violent felonies under Wyo. Stat. § 6-1-104(a)(xii).
Aggravated homicide by vehicle; drug-induced homicide.
Sexual assault and related sexual offenses under Wyo. Stat. §§ 6-2-301 through 6-2-320.
Certain domestic battery offenses; child abuse; endangering children with controlled substances; incest; sexual exploitation of children.
Aggravated assault or battery on a corrections or detention officer; disarming a peace officer; escape from official detention and violent or armed escape.
Bribery.
Weapons offenses under Wyo. Stat. §§ 6-8-101 and 6-8-102.
Any offense subject to sex offender registration under Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-19-302(g) through (j).
Felonies involving the use or attempted use of a firearm, except certain Title 23 offenses.
Any petitioner who has previously pled guilty or nolo contendere to, or been convicted of, a felony other than the felony or felonies being expunged.
Any person who has previously received an expungement of records of conviction under § 7-13-1502; the statute permits one in a lifetime.
Federal, tribal and out-of-state records, which Wyoming relief does not reach.

A completed deferral under Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-301 that ended in discharge and dismissal. Section 7-13-1502 opens "A person convicted of a felony", and Lynch v. State, 2026 WY 8 holds at ¶18 that a person who completed a deferral has no conviction and does not qualify.

destination.detail: File the verified petition and the proposed Order for Expungement with the clerk of the convicting court and pay the $300 filing fee per petition. The order is proposed and is generated unexecuted: its findings, its date, the judge's signature block and every clerk or court execution field are left blank, and nothing in it asserts that the court has acted. It is prepared so it is available to the court; whether it goes in with the initial filing or is brought later is that court's filing practice.

Filing, fee, service and timing sheet, including the $300 fee, the two service recipients, the 90-day objection window, the four-month minimum engagement, the § 7-13-1502(j) immunity provision, and the once-per-lifetime disclosure. No civil summons and no praecipe are required on this route under the statewide statutes and published guidance, and neither is generated. _remainingEligibilityRuleEncoding.basis: Every conclusion below is restructured from those two integrated decision records. No primary source was retrieved for this amendment and nothing is asserted that neither record establishes.

routesEnumeratedAndWhyEachFails: W.S. 7-13-1401, expungement of records of arrest, dismissal of charges and disposition — barred on its face. Subsection (a)(i) requires that there were no dispositions pursuant to W.S. 7-13-301 to any charge arising from the incident, including dispositions to a different or lesser charge, and repeats the exclusion for W.S. 35-7-1037 and former W.S. 7-13-203. A completed deferral is precisely such a disposition.

W.S. 7-13-1502 — requires a conviction. The section opens "A person convicted of a felony", and Lynch holds at ¶18 that a person who completed a deferral has none. At ¶15 the Court gives the reason the two sections read differently: the legislature did not need to exclude deferrals from § 7-13-1502 because that statute only allows the expungement of convictions.

W.S. 7-13-301 itself — contains no record-clearing provision. Subsections (a) through (f) cover probation terms, discharge and dismissal, revocation, the not-a-conviction-for-any-purpose rule at (d), the one-deferral-per-person rule at (e) and a commercial-driver exclusion at (f). Nothing about records.

W.S. 7-13-307 — forecloses the argument expressly: nothing in W.S. 7-13-301 through 7-13-306 shall be construed to authorize the court to expunge the record of a person charged with or convicted of a criminal offense. This is a statutory prohibition on the very construction a participant would want.

W.S. 7-12-310 and W.S. 7-12-404, post-conviction DNA testing and factual innocence — both operate on a conviction and both require actual or factual innocence. Neither reaches a person with no conviction to vacate.
W.S. 7-19-405, DNA database expungement — removes a sample and profile from the state database and touches neither the court record nor the criminal history record.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Approved for implementation with limitations and a manual-review gate. Three facts drove that and two of them survive intact: the § 7-13-1502 exclusion list is long, statute-specific and still not encoded, and the other-felony bar looks at the petitioner's whole record, which LegalEase cannot see. The third, that the restoration-of-rights effect under subsection (m) makes this the highest-value single filing in Wyoming and it should not be attempted on thin facts, is unaffected by any encoding. The ninety-day objection window also makes a Wyoming felony petition a four-month engagement at minimum, and the participant should be told so. What this amendment settles is the deferral population: the integrated governing-mechanism decision proves by enumeration that nothing in Wyoming law reaches a completed felony deferral and that W.S. 7-13-307 forbids reading the power into the deferral statutes, so that is now an encoded exclusion, a participant question and a fail-closed stop rather than an open build-level question. The Lynch citation is confirmed. The attorney-review gate is not removed: it was never standing in for the deferral answer alone.

limitations.statement: The § 7-13-1502 exclusion list is long and statute-specific and is not encoded. Do not offer this track without attorney review of whether the felony appears on the list. tracks.legalName: Motion to Vacate Conviction under Wyo. Stat. § 6-2-708(c) (human-trafficking victim)

controllingAuthority.summary: Wyo. Stat. § 6-2-708(c) expressly allows a motion at any time after entry of conviction, in the court where the conviction was entered, concerning the defendant's participation resulting from trafficking. The court may vacate; relief is discretionary, never written as mandatory. Government documentation of trafficking status creates a presumption but is not mandatory. Subsection (a) (defense to liability), subsection (b) (minors) and subsection (c) (post-conviction motion) are distinct; an unresolved pending charge is never routed into a conviction-vacatur instrument. The subsection adds no sentence-completion requirement, extra waiting period, trafficker conviction, automatic record destruction, $300 filing fee, or the 90-day DCI-notice process of the separate felony-expungement route.
